core: the working definition of risk in finance: the chance that actual results differ from expected results
the general risk-return relationship (higher expected return comes with higher risk)
the four named risk types: market risk, business risk, credit risk, inflation risk
variability as the basic idea behind measuring risk: wider swings mean more risk
risk tolerance: different investors and businesses accept different levels
managing risk: diversification, information, and time
the honest framing: risk cannot be avoided, only understood and priced
supporting: systematic versus unsystematic risk categorization (market risk as systematic)
standard deviation named as the common volatility metric, without formula depth
time horizon as a factor in risk tolerance
risk as two-sided: outcomes can be better or worse than expected
outOfScope: return measurement and calculation (sibling topic: finance:foundations:return)
diversification mechanics and portfolio construction (sibling topic: finance:foundations:diversification)
any investment advice or product recommendations

claims.claim: In finance, risk refers to the degree of uncertainty and/or potential financial loss inherent in an investment decision (Investor.gov); the working definition used in this lesson is CFI's: risk is the probability that actual results will differ from expected results, echoed by Investopedia's 'chance that actual gains will differ from an expected outcome or return'.
Higher expected returns generally come with higher risk: as investment risks rise, investors seek higher returns to compensate themselves for taking such risks.

Market risk (systematic risk) is the risk that factors affecting the overall market, such as political or macroeconomic events, pull many investments down at the same time; it is not easily mitigated through portfolio diversification alone.
Business risk is the risk that a company will not generate enough sales and revenue to cover its operational expenses and remain in business.
Credit risk is the risk that a borrower will be unable to pay the contractual interest or principal on its debt obligations.
Inflation risk is the risk that a general upward movement of prices erodes purchasing power, which is a particular concern for investors receiving a fixed rate of interest.

Risk is measured by the variability (volatility) of returns: returns that vary widely from year to year are considered risky, and the standard deviation of returns is the most commonly used measure of that volatility.
Risk tolerance differs across investors and businesses, based on factors such as age, income, goals, and how soon money is needed; there is no single correct level of tolerance.

Diversification is a method of reducing unsystematic (specific) risk by investing in a number of different assets, so that if one investment underperforms, the others balance it out; longer time horizons can make higher-risk investments more tolerable, and understanding risks helps manage them.
All investments involve some degree of risk; risk is two-sided (unexpected outcomes can be better or worse than expected) and cannot be eliminated, only understood, managed, and priced.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame the definition differently: Investor.gov emphasizes uncertainty and potential financial loss, while CFI and Investopedia emphasize the chance of results differing from expectations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the framings as complementary and attributes each to its source; the working definition follows CFI's 'actual results differ from expected results' phrasing, with Investor.gov's uncertainty framing as the supporting Tier A view.

rightsIssues: All four sources used REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose reproduced. OpenStax Principles of Finance disallows AI ingestion (aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map), so its content was read via an Internet Archive capture and restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Risk: What It Means in Investing, How to Measure and Manage It
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary; JS-walled live, so verified via Internet Archive snapshot 2024-01-01 on 2026-08-21). Supports: risk as the chance that an outcome or investment's actual gains will differ from an expected outcome or return, including the possibility of losing some or all of an original investment; standard deviation as a common risk metric measuring volatility of asset prices; market risk (systematic) as risk affecting an entire market or a large percentage of it, not easily mitigated by diversification; credit risk as the risk that a borrower will be unable to pay contractual interest or principal; business risk as whether a company can generate sufficient sales and revenue to cover operating expenses; risk-return tradeoff (low risk associated with low potential returns, high risk with high potential returns); risk tolerance differing by age, income, goals, and liquidity needs; time horizon as a key factor in risk assessment. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
